correctness.rationale: Exact polynomial Lanczos identity yields y_m(t)=p_(m-1,t)(A)b, with interpolation at Ritz nodes. Strict Ritz upper bound follows because a Krylov polynomial of degree <m cannot isolate L when m<s. Hermite–Genocchi integral gives p_(m-1,t)(x)e^(tx)=1−(−1)^m H_m(t,x), where H_m=t^m prod(x−theta_j)∫_{Delta_m}exp[t Σu_j(x−theta_j)]du. For x>theta_m, H_m grows continuously and strictly from 0 to infinity as t rises; odd m then remains positive while even m crosses uniquely, and H_m grows with extrapolation x, yielding decreasing crossing times. Lagrange coefficients show top-mode relative error has sign (−1)^(m−1) and diverges exponentially at rate L−theta1. Independent interpolation sign tests covered 6 depths; the analytic simplex argument proves the arbitrary-depth result.
residual_risks: Only the largest physical eigenvalue coordinate and monotonicity above all Ritz nodes; odd m does NOT imply positivity in every physical coordinate.

value.rationale: The approximation targets a positivity-preserving semigroup but truncation can lose positivity. The theorem gives a complete all-depth parity classification at the stiffest physical eigenmode, a unique time threshold at every even depth, and demonstrates that odd-depth sign preservation is compatible with exponentially bad relative accuracy. This is a directly motivated structural warning for Lanczos exponentials, not an arbitrary parameter slice.
residual_risks: No general componentwise positivity result outside the extreme eigenmode, exact arithmetic and diagonal matrices.

final_claim: For incomplete symmetric Lanczos approximation of positive diagonal exponential actions, the extreme physical eigenmode is positive at all times for odd Krylov dimensions, but has one strictly monotone sign loss for even dimensions; high-extrapolation crossing occurs sooner at larger eigenvalues, while relative errors grow exponentially.
limitations: Published m=2 horizon is already known; novelty scope only m odd and m even at least 4.
Classic interpolation is not itself novel and may imply the sign dichotomy in earlier literature.
